fatal_errors: The proposed intervention changes bulk Cr, Ni, and Mo concentrations rather than applying and annealing an AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy coating on SS316L.
The specified high-temperature, high-pressure aqueous environment does not reconstruct either the 3.5 wt% H2SO4 electrochemical test or the 900 °C cyclic molten-salt exposures.
Cr, Ni, and Mo are varied together, so the experiment cannot identify which element—or interaction among them—is the governing cause.
Self-healing is asserted without a film-disruption and time-resolved repassivation measurement.
E2 concerns Ti-Ta alloys in simulated body fluid and does not support the proposed mechanism in high-alloy steels or nuclear/chemical-processing environments.
explanation: The hypothesis is a scientifically plausible generic passivation account and includes a baseline, electrochemical measurements, surface analysis, boundaries, and a stated falsification criterion. It has limited mechanistic overlap with the target through Cr-rich oxide/hydroxide passivation and the prediction of increased polarization resistance. However, it misses the central material system, processing intervention, annealing optimum, grain and phase mediators, and the relevant acid and molten-salt conditions. E1 supports the existence of mixed oxide/hydroxide passive films on an Al-containing multicomponent coating, but it does not establish that jointly increasing Cr, Ni, and Mo causes thicker or self-healing films. The design could test a broad alloy-composition hypothesis, but factorial or single-element variations and deliberate scratch/repassivation testing would be required to identify the governing cause.
